title: Tomato leaf classifier (demo)
task: Classifies a photo of one tomato leaf into 10 classes: 9 diseases or pests, or healthy.

model.name: MobileNetV3-Small
model.head: Global average pooling, dropout 0.2, dense softmax over 10 classes
model.training: First the new layer alone for 2 rounds (epochs), then the whole network for 6 more at a small, decaying learning rate; the best round on the validation photos (round 5) was kept. About 110 minutes on a laptop CPU, no GPU.
model.augmentation: Each training photo is randomly cropped, flipped, turned and lightened or darkened, so the model can't just memorise how the dataset's photos were framed.

details.augmentation: random square crop of 70-100% of the short side, horizontal and vertical flips, rotation up to +/-29 degrees (reflect fill), brightness and contrast +/-15%

input.preprocessing: Centre square crop, resized to 224 x 224 RGB, values 0-255 as float32 (the model rescales them to -1..1 itself).

output: Softmax probabilities over 10 classes, in the order of labels.json

files.runtime: @tensorflow/tfjs-core + tfjs-converter 4.22.0, WebGL backend, CPU backend fallback

dataset.name: PlantVillage, tomato leaves (colour images)
dataset.licenceSource: Hughes & Salathé (2015), arXiv:1511.08060: images released under CC BY-SA 3.0 Unported, 'with the clarification that algorithms trained on the data fall under the same license'.
citation: D. P. Hughes and M. Salathé, An open access repository of images on plant health to enable the development of mobile disease diagnostics, arXiv:1511.08060, 2015.
S. P. Mohanty, D. P. Hughes and M. Salathé, Using deep learning for image-based plant disease detection, Frontiers in Plant Science 7:1419, 2016. doi:10.3389/fpls.2016.01419
dataset.split: 80/10/10 per class, by leaf: the dataset's leaf map (leaf_grouping/leaf-map.json), 'Leaf N' names, and blocks of 20 consecutive photo numbers for unmapped camera series, so photos of one leaf never cross splits (seed 1307). Stricter than the dataset's own 80/20 split, which leaves 37% of tomato photos ungrouped.

test.measured: These files, TensorFlow.js 4.22.0 (wasm backend) in Node, images resized to 224 x 224 with sharp. Read once, after the format was chosen on the validation photos.

licence.samples: CC BY-SA 3.0 (PlantVillage photos, re-encoded as WebP)
licence.why: The dataset's terms put algorithms trained on it under the same licence.

limits: PlantVillage photos show single leaves, picked and laid on a plain grey or black sheet, shot outdoors in daylight; leaves on the plant, busy backgrounds or other lighting will fool it more often.
It only knows these ten classes, so a photo of another plant, another disease or no leaf at all still gets one of them, sometimes with high confidence.
Test accuracy is measured on PlantVillage photos only, so it says little about photos from a field.
notThePaper: Not the model from Comparative Performance of Deep Learning Algorithms in Tomato Disease Detection (IEEE CONIT 2025): a separate, much smaller model trained for this page.
